newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Amnesty International criticises SAfrica on Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty International criticises SAfrica on Rwanda.

text.p: Human rights group Amnesty International on Saturday criticised South Africa's decision to resume arms sales to Rwanda, saying Pretoria was ignoring grave human rights violations in the Central African country.
South Africa said on Wednesday it was lifting a ban on arms sales to Rwanda after receiving assurances that no weapons would be used abroad.
The London-based human rights group said in a statement that South Africa had said it would take human rights protection seriously when deciding on exports of military hardware.
Amnesty said Pretoria should not resume arms sales to Rwanda until the country's army has shown that it has stopped committing atrocities.

"However, it is clear that atrocities against civilians have been committed by the Rwandese Patriotic Army (RPA) in former Zaire and in Rwanda itself -- atrocities which the Rwandese government denies. There is no reason why the South African government should believe these latest assurances," Amnesty added.

Pretoria suspended a deal worth 87 million rand ($19 million) in November after reports that Rwandan troops were involved in the rebellion in next-door Zaire which eventually toppled president Mobutu Sese Seko.
South African officials have refused to detail the types of arms offered for sale, describing them merely as "defensive" but Amnesty said the deal included armoured vehicles and military radios.
"Any government which supplies lethal weapons to armed forces that use them to kill unarmed civilians should accept part of the responsibility for the killings which ensue," Amnesty added.

Laurent Kabila's Tutsi-dominated rebellion in the former Zaire led to the repatriation of around a million Rwandan Hutus. They had fled to camps in then Zaire in 1994 after Hutu extremists massacred several hundred thousand Tutsi countrymen in a genocide.
Since their return home, killings and political instability in now Tutsi-controlled Rwanda have increased.
